newsitem.title: INDIA: India plans tough new law against child sex.
newsitem.headline: India plans tough new law against child sex.

text.p: India plans to introduce a stringent law against paedophilia to protect children against sexual abuse, Health Minister Renuka Chowdhury said on Thursday.
She said the law would be similar to that passed by Australia, where paedophiles face up to 17 years in jail and can be prosecuted at home for offences abroad.

Children's rights activists say nearly one third of the sex workers in six major Indian cities are under the age of 20. The privately-funded Indian Health Organisation in Bombay says around 1,000 girls a year are initiated into prostitution.

Human rights groups say neighbouring Sri Lanka, which relies on tourism as a main source of foreign exchange and employment, has become a popular destination for paedophiles. The island nation, which lies south of India, in 1995 passed tough laws aimed at discouraging foreign tourists seeking sex with children and put police on alert for paedophiles.

The law calls for a minimum five years in jail and a maximum 20-year sentence for pimps and their clients. It raised the minimum age of consent to 18 for boys and 16 for girls, making sex with anyone under those ages a crime.

"We are asking for information from different countries on their laws before making ours," a Health Ministry spokesman told Reuters. He said the new law would target mainly foreigners but gave no other details.

A British charity, Christian Aid, says some 200,000 Nepali girls have been sold into sexual slavery in Indian brothels. It estimates some 60,000 children work as prostitutes in the Philippine sex industry and up to 200,000 in Thailand.

Chowdhury said children in India were becoming increasingly vulnerable to AIDS, with nearly 80 percent of those with the disease dying within five years of infection due to their low resistance levels.

Chowdhury said about 125 AIDS patients under the age of 14 were still alive, representing about four percent of India's AIDS cases. "Though the number looks small now, the graph is going up," she said.

Nearly 100 are boys, which indicates that people are either ashamed of reporting that their daughters are infected with a sexually transmitted disease, or that they prefer to neglect the girl child, the minister said. Most catch HIV from their mothers while still in the womb.

The government also plans to install condom-vending machines in restaurants, cinema halls, petrol pumps and roadside food stalls, where long-distance truck drivers often stop and pick up prostitutes, the minister said.
Government statistics show that nearly 53,000 Indians are infected with HIV, which causes Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome. More than 3,500 people are estimated to have AIDS.
But World Health Organisation officials say AIDS is carried by some 1.5 million Indians and at least five million could be infected with HIV by the end of the century.
Health Ministry officials say AIDS reached India in the early 1990s, and the country's dense population, poverty, and high illiteracy rate turned it into a hidden but explosive epidemic.

They say AIDS is transmitted mainly through heterosexual sex in India. Intravenous drug abuse, migrant workers, a trucking industry criss-crossing the country, prostitution, and social taboos against talking about sex have also aided its spread.
